citations.quote: I used to ask in interview, you can also listen to this, why call stack is actually a stack? Why can't call stack be actually linked list or why not call stack be tree?

patterns.observation: Vasanth uses a rhetorical question to explain why the call stack is a stack and not another data structure like a linked list or tree.

proposed_adaptation.action: Use rhetorical questions to provoke critical thinking about why specific data structures are used over others.
proposed_adaptation.limits: Avoid overuse where direct explanation is more suitable.
proposed_adaptation.when: Explaining data structure concepts in programming tutorials

patterns.qualification: Self-reported in a recorded transcript. No independent observation or broader application verified.
patterns.situation: Vasanth uses rhetorical questions during a programming lesson on YouTube to discuss the nature of call stack and different data structures.

citations.quote: If execution happens that way, then the d will be printed first, because it's a stack, right? It's a pile of plates, one one on top of another.

patterns.observation: Explains the concept of the call stack using the analogy of a pile of plates to demonstrate the LIFO (Last In First Out) order.

proposed_adaptation.action: Use relatable analogies like comparing a stack to a pile of plates to convey LIFO principles.
proposed_adaptation.limits: Not applicable for detailed algorithmic behavior requiring precise technical vocabulary.
proposed_adaptation.when: Introducing stack data structure concepts to programming students

patterns.qualification: Limited to an individual speaker's analogy in an isolated lesson. No cross-case validation.
patterns.situation: During a programming lecture, the speaker uses an analogy to explain the last-in-first-out behavior of the call stack in JavaScript.
